\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}

\title{Fourier Analysis for Communications: Week 3}
\author{Course Team}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{The Channel Model}
We model the received waveform as a scaled, delayed, and
noisy copy of the transmitted symbol waveform. Writing
$s(t)$ for the transmitted signal and $h(t)$ for the
impulse response of the channel, the derivation of the
received signal, its transform, and its average power runs
as follows:
\begin{align*}
s(t) &= A \cos(2\pi f_c t + \phi) + n(t) \\
\hat{s}(t) &= s(t) * h(t) \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} s(\tau) h(t - \tau) \, d\tau \\
S(f) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} s(t) e^{-j 2\pi f t} \, dt \\
|S(f)|^2 &= S(f) \, S^{*}(f) \\
P &= \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |s(t)|^2 \, dt
\end{align*}
Each line follows from the previous one by the convolution
theorem or by Parseval's identity, and the last line defines
the average power over one symbol period.

\section{Why One Derivation}
The six lines above are a single logical chain, and the
exercises will ask you to reproduce them in order. Skipping
the convolution step is the most common error: the received
waveform is not the product of $s(t)$ and $h(t)$, whatever
the notation in some older handouts suggests. The transform
line is where the Fourier machinery enters, and the power
line is where the symbol period $T$ finally appears.

\section{Common Errors}
Do not confuse the dummy variable of integration with the
time variable of the output: mixing $\tau$ and $t$ in the
convolution integral corrupts every later line. And do not
drop the complex conjugate in the energy spectrum; the
spectrum is real by construction, but only because the
conjugate is there.

\section{Reading}
The course text covers convolution in chapter 4 and the
energy spectrum in chapter 5. The notation $S^{*}(f)$ for
the conjugate is the author's, and we keep it here for
consistency with the exercises.

\section{Exercises}
For the tutorial, verify the power line for the case where
$s(t)$ is a single rectangular pulse of unit height, and
compute the relative error committed by truncating the
Fourier integral at the tenth harmonic. Then redo the
convolution line for a channel whose impulse response is
a pure delay of half a symbol period, and check that the
power line is unchanged, as Parseval's identity demands.
\end{document}
